articles.title: Election posters, mass tourism and property: Israel’s footprint in Cyprus
articles.summary: Cypriots say Israeli money is moving fast and shutting them out as their government embraces Israel as a key ally.
articles.body:
Various locations, Cyprus – This summer in Cyprus, on a road near Larnaca airport, a billboard greeted holidaymakers in Hebrew: “Israelis, enjoy! Now come back and win!”

It was an election poster in the Cypriot city for Israel’s October 27 vote featuring Israel’s former army chief and leader of the opposition Yashar Party, Gadi Eisenkot.

The poster of Eisenkot, believed to be the first time a foreign politician had campaigned on billboards in Cyprus, signalled the growing number of Israelis living on and visiting the island, TV presenter and pro-Palestine activist Melanie Steliou told Al Jazeera.

“Israel is only 40 minutes away by plane; they can pop over, vote, and come back within the day,” she said.

Israel does not allow most citizens living abroad to vote outside the country, so campaigns court those who can fly home on polling day.

The poster demonstrates how Israeli politicians see Cyprus as “just another district of Israel”, Steliou said.

Israeli political influence is also being felt in Cyprus’s parliament. On October 20, six Cypriot lawmakers formed a pro-Israel caucus, launched by the advocacy group Israel Allies Foundation, The Jerusalem Post reported.

Cyprus has absorbed waves of foreign buyers before. Limassol was once nicknamed “Limassolgrad” for its Russian community.

Theodosis Pipis, a Cypriot historian and analyst with the think tank KEDISA, said that with Russian investment in the early 2010s, “you saw big buildings pop up” as companies moved over but “you never really saw a huge influx of buying houses, building schools, creating communities.”

Waves of foreign money before had not shaped the island’s political climate or brought foreign election campaigns with it, he said. Israeli investment, by contrast, is creating “a sense of community for the future”, he explained.

Israelis made nearly 600,000 trips to Cyprus last year, more than double the 2022 figure, according to the Cyprus Statistical Service (CYSTAT). In August, nearly one in four tourists arriving on the island was Israeli, a 28.4 percent increase from 2025, according to CYSTAT, with some buying homes .

In the 12 months to September 2025, Israelis made 850 property purchases in Larnaca district, more than any other foreign nationality, according to Ministry of Interior data. Israel’s embassy in Nicosia estimates that 15,000 to 20,000 consider the island home, Cypriot news outlet Philenews reported in August. According to the last census in 2021, slightly more than 1,000 Israelis lived in or were registered in Cyprus.

Venetians, Ottomans and the British all held the island before independence in 1960. It has been divided since Turkiye’s 1974 invasion, which followed a coup backed by the military government in Athens.

More recently, British retirees, Russian capital and golden-passport buyers have poured money into its property market.

But the speed, scale and nature of new Israeli investments, to an island where walls are covered in pro-Palestine murals and graffiti amid the genocide in Gaza , have caught the attention of many.

Investment from Israel rose more than sixfold between 2017 and 2024, to 5.1 billion euros ($5.9bn), according to the Central Bank of Cyprus, even as total foreign investment in the country fell by a quarter between 2022 and 2024 and Russian holdings, much of it money simply routed through Cypriot holding companies, shrank by more than a third.

Nasia Hadjigeorgiou, an associate professor in transitional justice and human rights at the University of Central Lancashire in Cyprus, told Al Jazeera that British and Lebanese buying “wasn’t something that made waves” and “came almost naturally”. The Israeli push, by contrast, “was a more sudden development”.

That timing matters, Hadjigeorgiou said. Israel’s government keeps receiving “a lot of cover and a lot of support” from Nicosia at a time when Israel “is doing unspeakable things” in the Palestinian enclave, “and that makes at least a portion of the population uncomfortable.”

Steliou pulled out her phone and showed one video – footage of a person who had been dining at an Israeli-owned restaurant attempting to attack protesters at a pro-Palestine march in Cyprus. Then another – an Israeli man writing expletives, drawing a sexual organ and spitting on a mural honouring Gaza’s children.

Amid Israel’s wars on Gaza and Lebanon, locals interviewed by Al Jazeera said the presence of Israelis who had served in the military was hard to bear.

“I feel my heart sink when I hear and see large groups of Israeli men here, knowing that they have served in the military and can commit genocide and then buy property,” Giorgos Kyrou, a 32-year-old artist from Limassol, said.

“Our politicians are compromised,” said Ioannis Nestoras, a potter who lives in Limassol. “They are willing to hug, to embrace, to treat as friends the Israeli government … I don’t think it’s representative of the Cypriot mentality.”

Outside the NYX Hotel Limassol, owned by Fattal, Israel’s largest hotel group, Steliou said Israeli investment appears centred on residential zones, including so-called “gated communities”.

Politicians, estate agents, academics and residents in Cyprus use the phrase to describe clusters of Israeli-owned properties they see as closed off from the wider community.

No official count exists, and owners’ nationalities are not recorded for purchases through Cypriot companies.

But patterns are visible. Israeli companies have bought most of the coastline between Livadia and Pyla, near Larnaca, to build homes and hotels, the Cypriot financial news site Stockwatch reported last year.

Stockwatch also reported that Israeli investors are promoting the largest organised residential development in Cyprus in Dromolaxia-Meneou, near Larnaca, with its own kindergarten, swimming pools, and private park.

Other Cypriots share Steliou’s concerns.

Kyrou said Israeli investments can focus on a particular area and that “sometimes it feels like the locals are being pushed out of those villages or urban centres”.

As a historian, Pipis said he understood fears that Israel’s occupation of Palestine could be repeated, though he did not expect that in Cyprus. Instead, he believes a foothold in a friendly EU member state “offers a certain safety if things escalate more in the Middle East”.

“You don’t buy these amounts of land preparing to create communities with schools … if you’re not planning to stay there for the long term,” he said.

In Polemidia, on the edge of Limassol, the Yael Foundation is funding a “flagship Jewish school” for up to 1,500 pupils, due to open in 2027. Cyprus has many private and international schools serving foreign communities.

Rabbi Yehoshua Smukler, who leads the project, has described this one as a “Zionist school”.

Critics also point to a pattern of building first and seeking permission later.

In February 2025, Cyprus’s Ministry of Education said that no application had been submitted for the school, and as late as October that year, the Ministry of Finance said the application was still being finalised, the Cypriot daily Kathimerini reported. Polemidia’s municipality, which complained it was not consulted, had itself been refused permission to build a sport centre on the same plot, the newspaper said.

The ministry did not respond to Al Jazeera’s questions.

In addition to schools, other infrastructure catering to Israelis has popped up.

Hadassah, one of the biggest hospital groups in Israel, owned by the US group “Hadassah, The Women’s Zionist Organization of America”, opened its first European medical centre in Limassol in July.

“Specific areas are being bought en masse”, Stefanos Stefanou, leader of the left-wing Cypriot AKEL Party, said in June 2025. Purchases in Larnaca and Limassol were creating gated communities “almost inaccessible to anyone other than Israeli nationals”, he said, adding that Israel is preparing a “backyard” in Cyprus.

“We do not say this because of xenophobia or anti-Semitism,” he later said.

Israel’s former Ambassador to Cyprus Oren Anolik hit back, saying Stefanou’s comments sought to “single out the Jewish community in Cyprus”.

Hadjigeorgiou said there was likely “some exaggeration in relation to some of the examples” of closed-off areas, but that some were “very clearly gated communities”.

Speaking as a lawyer, she said Cyprus’s constitution and the European Convention on Human Rights prohibit discrimination on grounds including ethnicity, nationality and religion and that a development where only Israelis can buy “is unconstitutional”.

In western Cyprus, Uriel Kertesz, a businessman with Hungarian and Israeli citizenship, bought an estimated 70 to 80 percent of the abandoned village of Trozena and its surrounding farmland, which lies in a protected area. Yiannis Pazouros, a journalist at the Cypriot daily Politis who investigated the purchases and met Kertesz, said buying as an EU citizen freed him from limits on non-EU buyers.

Kertesz paid double or triple the market value and pushed ahead without the permits needed in a protected area, Pazouros said. Al Jazeera cannot independently confirm this.

Despite public fears that the village could be closed off, Kertesz has stayed tight-lipped about his plans, he added.

Criticism of Israel is far from uncommon in Cyprus, particularly in light of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.

Recently, on an October evening, Mike Kroll, an Israeli-American comedian based in Tel Aviv, played at a comedy festival in Limassol.

It initially caused “apprehension” because of Israel’s image, he said.

He felt “fine” with people criticising Israel because he was treated with respect and had engaged in “deep discussions”.

However, his reaction has not been not universal.

Across Cyprus, pro-Palestinian slogans turn public spaces into expressions of solidarity. Some are more direct in their meaning: “Zionists not welcome” reads graffiti in Larnaca.

In August 2025, after Israel’s Diaspora Affairs Minister Amichai Chikli complained to Cypriot ministers, the Interior Ministry ordered municipalities to remove what it called hate-inciting graffiti.

In Limassol, crews removed it with uncharacteristic efficiency, sometimes before 6am, Nestoras said. The mayor initially tried to protect it as political expression but was overruled, fuelling suspicion the order came from “higher-ups”.

The Interior Ministry did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.

For Cypriots, Hadjigeorgiou said, the changes carry particular weight.

“We are a population that has been displaced from our homes in what the government loudly and clearly describes as ethnic cleansing. And at the same time, we are allowing another group to do the same thing in the areas that the Republic of Cyprus controls.”

articles.title: Four ways Labour could raise money in the Budget without hiking income tax
articles.summary: Chancellor John Healey may need to raise money to boost his fiscal headroom - BBC Verify examines what options could be on the table.
articles.body:
We're likely to hear a lot about the chancellor's "headroom" in this Budget.

That is the cash buffer the government has to help meet its own fiscal rules and reduce borrowing.

Economists think the buffer might have halved in the last six months from around £24bn to as low as £11bn, in part because of rising interest rates the government has been paying to borrow money from private investors.

The Chancellor, John Healey, might need to raise money to restore it, which would show the government's plan to reduce borrowing by the end of this Parliament is still on track.

At the same time, he is under pressure to find money to help people with the rising cost of living and to fund spending on defence. However, Labour's 2024 election manifesto pledged not to raise the rates of income tax, VAT or National Insurance.

Increasing taxes on capital gains or extending the mansion tax had been raised as possible options but have since been ruled out by government sources.

BBC Verify has looked at what other options could be on the table for the chancellor to raise some more money on Wednesday.

Banks in the UK have seen profits rise in recent years because they have been able to charge people higher interest rates when borrowing money.

And there is widespread belief among bank bosses that the chancellor is preparing to raise taxes on banks in this week's Budget.

Think tank Tax Policy Associates estimates that increasing the surcharge that banks pay on corporation tax from 3% to 5.5% could potentially raise an additional £1bn to £2bn a year for the Treasury.

A higher tax would initially reduce the profits that banks have to distribute to their shareholders.

Some shareholders will be wealthy investors. The banks have warned that additional taxes could deter them from investing in the UK , which could reduce jobs.

And ordinary savers could be indirectly affected too, if their pension investments include bank shares .

Banks could also pass some of the tax burden on to their customers by offering lower savings rates or higher borrowing costs, research suggests.

Former Prime Minister Gordon Brown has called on Healey to hike the tax on electronic gaming machines - such as those found in betting shops and adult gaming centres which can offer payouts of £500 per game - citing the social harm imposed by problem gambling.

The Social Market Foundation (SMF) think tank has estimated that doubling tax on these machines from 20% to 40% could raise could raise between £275m and £460m - depending on how gamblers reacted to it.

People who use gambling machines could also end up having the tax passed on to them through worse odds on games, though anti-gambling groups argue this could help discourage more people from using them.

Research from the SMF found that gambling machines are increasingly clustered on some of the UK's most deprived high streets, and that one in four people who play casino games on these machines gamble at risky or harmful levels.

The gambling industry has argued such a tax hike could cause betting shops, which own and operate the machines, to close down, by making them less profitable.

It has also argued that betting shop closures could reduce the money bookmakers contribute to horse racing , potentially putting jobs in that industry at risk too.

3. Get online marketplaces to collect VAT

Reports suggest the chancellor is preparing to announce that big online marketplaces such as Amazon, Ebay and Temu will be made responsible for collecting tax owed by retailers selling on their platforms.

The Treasury estimates it is missing out on around £12bn a year in VAT revenues that should be paid by companies, which it calls the "VAT tax gap".

Tax experts say that part of the problem - although not accounting for the full £12bn of the VAT gap - is that some online sellers fail to comply with VAT rules, either by not charging VAT when they should or by failing to pass on VAT collected from customers to the government.

Enforcement can be difficult because some firms that use platforms like Amazon to sell their products are based overseas and falsely present themselves as UK-established businesses.

Others close down and reopen under different company names to escape their tax liabilities.

Reports suggest that this move to make big online marketplaces responsible for collecting the tax - rather than the individual retailers - would clamp down on this form of tax evasion and could raise around £1bn in extra VAT a year.

Amazon, which supports the move, has estimated it could raise £700m a year in VAT for the government.

Some sellers could respond by raising prices or leaving the platform, which could have an impact on some shoppers.

However, it would also level the playing field for online sellers, ensuring those businesses who charge VAT are not illegally undercut by those who break the rules and do not.

The above three tax measures together would raise a maximum of only around £3.5bn a year.

That would be small relative to the sums of money the chancellor might well need to restore his headroom and pay for any new spending.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said in the summer he wanted a "fair and lasting" reduction to the UK's welfare bill, while the government is under pressure from opposition parties to find savings from working-age benefits.

The Conservatives claim they could make savings of £36bn a year by restricting people's access to welfare payments.

Reform say they would save £50bn a year in this way, although independent analysts say there are questions about how realistic it is to make such large savings.

Working health and sickness benefits have risen sharply since the Covid pandemic and the overall cost is projected by the Office for Budget Responsibility to increase from £68bn this year to £81bn in 2031.

Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves attempted to reduce spending on these benefits by £5bn a year by 2030, but were forced to reverse course after a revolt by backbench Labour MPs.

Independent welfare experts and economists say savings from the working age welfare budget are possible but would likely require upfront spending to help people into work, which could cancel out any near-term savings for the Treasury.

Cuts to health and disability welfare would reduce the incomes of people who currently receive those payments and/or those who would otherwise receive them in future - and campaigners warn of the risk of people being pushed into poverty.

However, if more welfare claimants were also supported into work, their overall incomes could be maintained or even rise.

articles.title: I lost my job in a primary school due to endometriosis
articles.summary: A new report says nearly half of women with endometriosis have lost income due to the condition.
articles.body:
Hayley Locksley was 11 years old when she started her periods and excruciating pain became part of her life.

"I used to spend every month in the sick room at school," she says.

Hayley, from Shefford, Bedfordshire, would often pass out from the pain but the doctors' advice was to take paracetamol.

Aged 24, she was diagnosed with endometriosis - a condition that affects one in 10 women, where tissue similar to the lining of the womb grows outside of the uterus.

Hayley says she loved her job working in a nursery, but her employers questioned whether her symptoms were real and asked her to use annual leave to cover sick days.

After she had surgery for endometriosis, Hayley decided to switch to office work, due to it being less physically demanding. But her new colleagues asked why she was spending so long in the toilet.

"I had to explain that my bladder sometimes did not empty fully, causing severe pain and horrendous diarrhoea. I found the questioning embarrassing and humiliating," she says.

After having her daughter, who is now aged seven, Hayley decided to pursue her dream of working with children again and became a special needs teaching assistant in a primary school four years ago.

However, she was placed under review after her sickness absence increased and she lost her job last October, after being told she was unfit to work.

"I didn't want to give up my career but my health meant I could no longer continue," she says.

"I now use a walking stick, experience severe back and leg pain, and have fallen numerous times. Losing my job has been so tough for my mental health," she adds.

Nearly half of women with endometriosis have lost income due to the condition, according to a new report by the All-Party Parliamentary Group on Endometriosis.

The inquiry found 97% had worked while in severe pain, 47% had lost income because of their symptoms, and 28% had left a job altogether.

Endometriosis surgeon Dr Rebecca Mallick says the figures are shocking, but not surprising.

"Women should not have to choose between their health and their careers. We have raised awareness for years. Now we need meaningful action," she says.

Carla Cressy worked as a model from the age of five until she was 17, but she kept collapsing on shoots and retrained as a self-employed beauty therapist.

The 35-year-old from Essex was diagnosed with endometriosis 10 years ago. Yet as it was left untreated for so long, it progressed into frozen pelvis disease and destroyed her reproductive organs, leaving her needing bladder reconstruction and a total hysterectomy.

Carla now runs the charity The Endometriosis Foundation and gave evidence to the inquiry.

"Having experienced first hand the impact endometriosis can have on your working life, I know just how difficult it can be. And these are things we hear about from our community every single day.

"People struggling to stay in work, taking time off for treatment, losing income and sometimes having to give up careers they've worked incredibly hard for.

"I really hope this isn't where the conversation ends. We need to keep the pressure on government to prioritise endometriosis care, but employers have a part to play too. Better understanding and support in the workplace can make such a difference to someone's life."

A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson agrees the condition can have a "devastating impact" on women's lives and says the inquiry's findings highlight the need for better support, both in healthcare and in the workplace.

Faye Ramsey, 32, from Ipswich, spent 10 years in agony, with doctors suggesting she had irritable bowel syndrome before she was finally diagnosed last year.

She had a hysterectomy in June and had her endometriosis removed but struggled mentally and physically to return to work as a teaching assistant.

Through her work as the founder of a support organisation called Girls Anatomy, Faye has met women who have lost their jobs, had their hours reduced, or been physically sick at work after "dragging themselves in...because they don't want to lose their jobs".

Faye, who also gave evidence to the inquiry, wants to see more endometriosis friendly recognised employers and better protection for women with the condition in their probation periods.

"It's not pleasant to try and fight for your job and justify why you're the way that you are and why you're having that time off," she says.

"Your absence policy shouldn't be the same as someone who is able-bodied and has no medical condition, you shouldn't be [judged] against that person because it's just not fair."

The government says it is working with employers to improve awareness of the condition.

More than 6,000 women were interviewed for the inquiry and 94% said employers lacked a good understanding of endometriosis, and half received no workplace adjustments.

Of the 250 employers surveyed, 72% said their organisation gives no training or guidance on women's health.

But Matthew Percival, the Confederation of British Industry's future of work and skills director, says businesses are "increasingly aware of women's health issues".

Firms are keen to explore how they can support women "without their careers being held back", in a "wider shift" towards helping improve health and wellbeing in the workplace, he adds.

Hayley, Carla and Faye all say they hope employers can show more understanding of endometriosis in the future.

They want women to be believed, treated with dignity and supported to remain in work.

"Behind every absence, every appointment and every person who struggles at work, there may be a much bigger story than they realise," Hayley says.

Hayley hopes she will be able to return to the classroom one day, but at the moment she knows it is not possible.

"Endometriosis has taken so much from me. I don't want to be in this position. I loved my job and I worked really hard. To be told at 40 years old that I'm not fit for work, I'm now left wondering, is that it for my working life?

"I'm still 25 years away from retirement age. Am I going to be able to ever work again?"

articles.title: Cambridge students swap Blu Tack and posters for original art
articles.summary: The scheme is run by Kettle's Yard and allows students to borrow one painting, drawing or print.
articles.body:
Students in Cambridge are ditching traditional posters and Blu Tack in favour of adorning their rooms with professional works of art.

For almost 70 years, Kettle's Yard gallery in Cambridge has loaned framed art, from creatives like Ai Weiwei, to students from the city's universities for a £20 fee.

Sarah Kleinmoedhie, 22, a Politics student at the University of Cambridge who was one of about 100 who collected a piece this year, said: "It makes for such a good conversation starter when your friends come to your room."

The museum has said every piece has been returned despite some being brought back later than planned, including one borrowed by Stephen Hawking.

Naomi Polonsky, Kettle's Yard assistant curator, said: "The reason we know he [Hawking] participated in this scheme is that he is listed in the log for late returns... it did eventually come back to Kettle's Yard."

The loan scheme was established by art collector and curator Jim Ede, who founded Kettle's Yard in the 1950s.

He believed "young people could be at home unhampered by the greater austerity of the museum or public art gallery".

Students from the University of Cambridge and Anglia Ruskin University visited the gallery on Monday.

The museum said more than 100 students lined up at its doors, but only 86 pieces were on offer.

Kleinmoedhie, who has borrowed one, added: "I just think artwork is such a special way to engage with the world around you, and it is so interesting to visit here."

The value of the artwork is not disclosed, although the pieces are not from the gallery's core collection.

Polonsky added: "It is remarkable that it has existed since that time and many students at the university write in with reminiscences, even when borrowing the artwork in the 1960s."

Polonsky said students from 29 out of the 31 colleges at the University of Cambridge collected a piece of artwork last year.

Students have to pay a £30 refundable deposit in case a piece is damaged or not returned.

Some of the pieces loaned out in 2026 included a limited edition print of Motorbike by surrealist artist Bevis Sale and a piece by the British painter and sculptor, Richard Harold Redvers Taylor, called Seville, The Old Quarter 1954.

New to the collection was Ai Weiwei's Cats limited print and Melanie Manchot's The Ladies, the museum said.

The gallery's assistant director, Susie Biller, said everything loaned since 1957 had been returned, adding: "We haven't honestly had any problems... in all of the years we have had the odd delay."

The museum said most pieces were covered by students' contents insurance, with the scheme otherwise operating on trust.

articles.title: Norfolk: Work house 250th anniversary to highlight care home past
articles.summary: The live history destination says it could be the last chance to record life after the workhouse shut.
articles.body:
A museum at a former Victorian workhouse is appealing for people's memories of the time when it was turned into a care home after World War Two.

Gressenhall Farm and Workhouse is based at buildings that date from 1777 which are celebrating their 250th anniversary next year.

In the 1940s, it was turned into a care home and renamed Beech House. It closed in 1975 with residents being moved to Holt and Costessey.

Curator Rachel Kidd said the anniversary might be the "last chance" to capture the accounts of people who lived, visited and worked there.

The workhouse was a place where people living in poverty/on the breadline could come and exchange physical labour for food and shelter.

Gabby Meadows, research and community co-ordinator at the museum, said: "As social care and healthcare was changing in the '40s with the development of the NHS, things were changing at Gressenhall.

"It was moving away from that kind of workhouse environment and becoming about offering support to families."

Despite the changes, Meadows said there still was a stigma attached to the site because of its time as a workhouse.

She is hoping that people who visited relatives at Beech House will come forward to share their memories.

The team has already had a number of people come forward to share their experiences.

Angela Almond's father was a religious minister in Dereham in the 1960s who would regularly visit Gressenhall and take her with him.

"I was very conscious that some of the residents didn't want to be here," she said.

"Not because they were not cared for or fed properly, but because they were of the generation that grew up while it was still a workhouse."

The workhouse site, which has a school, chapel and laundry, is a popular school trip location hosting hundreds of children from across the region.

Its history as a workhouse is brought to life by staff in costume.

Curator Rachel Kidd said they want to understand more about the contemporary history.

"We want to show that the health and welfare system changed a lot in those 200 years all in one building," she said.

"It really is important to remember to reflect on how we do that today."

The 250th anniversary commemorations are being funded by £131,916 from The National Lottery Heritage Fund and £11,500 from the Friends of Gressenhall.

articles.title: Budget 2026: No more fat to trim for 'squeezed middle'
articles.summary: As the chancellor finalises his first Budget, how are the "squeezed middle" feeling about costs?
articles.body:
As Chancellor John Healey puts the final touches to his first Budget, how are the "squeezed middle" feeling after years of cost-of-living pressure?

Dawn Fazackerley-King is trying to work out how she and her family will pay higher mortgage costs anticipated in a few months' time.

"There's just no more fat to trim," says the mother-of-two.

The interest rate on their Ipswich home loan could rise from 1.4% to about 5.3%, which, Dawn says, could add "about £250 extra a month just for living in the same property".

"We just have to find that money from somewhere, but when you look at the direct debits every month, there's nothing fancy in there," she adds.

The BBC has contacted HM Treasury for comment.

Dawn lists the usual monthly bills, including their mortgage, council tax and energy costs, adding "there's no regular meals out or anything like that".

Over the past few years of increasing costs, Dawn says her family – which includes two children aged six and eight – have been "trimming the fat accordingly".

"It's quite worrying... where that money is going to come from when we're already feeling that squeeze," she says.

Dawn, 42, works as a full-time self-employed Pilates instructor in Ipswich, while her husband works in an office and the couple have a household income of about £70,000 a year.

"Yes. Life is definitely getting more expensive," she says.

In August 55% of adults that responded to an Office for National Statistics survey said their cost of living had increased compared with the previous month.

That rate was lower than the 62% recorded in August 2025 and lower than the 79% who said so in April this year.

But with more than half of adults facing increased expenses, the rising cost of living appears to be more chronic – a long-term issue rather than a shorter-term crisis.

For those who said costs were up, the most common reasons were the price of food shopping, fuel and energy bills.

"I think we've come to accept that is just the way it is at the moment – and we're lucky that we're able to keep our heads above water," Dawn says.

In the summer Prime Minister Andy Burnham promised to create " breathing space " for households struggling with costs.

More recently Burnham announced plans to remove standing charges on gas bills .

What is Dawn's message to the prime minister and the chancellor?

"Please start listening. The cost of living is becoming unbearable and I don't feel that the government are always hearing that message."

While welcoming the move on standing charges, Dawn says ministers had been "trying to put sticking plasters over gaping wounds", which were "not fixing the problems".

The Office for Budget Responsibility, which independently analyses the UK's public finances, predicted " real household disposable income " would increase by an average of 0.75% a year between 2026 and 2030.

The same rate – which balances income, taxes and benefits, and costs – grew by an average of 3% a year between 2000 and 2007.

Ed Miliband has been credited with introducing the term "squeezed middle" into the political conversation, shortly after he became Labour leader in 2010.

The following year it was the Oxford English Dictionary's expression of the year , which defined it as "the section of society regarded as particularly affected by inflation, wage freezes and cuts in public spending during a time of economic difficulty".

The definition said to be "principally" made up of those on "low or middle incomes".

Jessica Taylor, 41, a single mum based in Clacton-on-Sea, Essex, says her income is about £26,000 a year.

She receives Universal Credit and says she too is "definitely" feeling the squeeze.

Jessica recalls explaining to her 11-year-old son that – while they have a good life – they're "poor in the sense that on paper we live month to month".

"If I lost my job, we've got one month – maybe two – and then we are the real poor," she adds.

She says she does "the really small things" to make her money go further.

They include scouring maps and satellite images to find streets where parking is unrestricted.

Before heading out, she says she spends "10 minutes in the bath on Google Earth going 'that road!'."

Jessica says she is "happy… content… grateful" for the life she and her son have, but adds: "I wish I could do more – I wish I could not panic if a car bill comes in, maybe not ask mum for help sometimes, which is rare.

"I wish that I could go on a few more holidays a year.

"But I sacrificed the holidays so that my son – throughout the year – can do regular days out, [have] regular experiences."

Jessica and her 62-year-old mum Karen Badenoch run Trusted Money Confidence, a community interest company that hosts free sessions for people to share money management advice and strategies.

Karen, who used to work in admin for an architecture practice, says they frequently see "people in work, racking up debts on credit cards and buy-now-pay-later just to be able to get to the end of the month".

"The biggest thing that anyone can do is be open... and look at what your issues are – and that way you can resolve them.

"It is a huge lift off your mind if you actually start dealing with things and facing up to them, and believe me – you're not alone."

Healey has promised the Budget will keep to Labour's commitment not to hike the three main taxes – income tax, National Insurance and VAT – while sticking to the party's fiscal rules.

He recently also said it would deliver "growth in every postcode, while giving businesses and families some breathing space".

Healey will deliver his first Budget on Wednesday when Dawn, Jessica and the rest of us will hear what he might do to ease the squeeze.

articles.title: Who Israel elects matters, and not just for Israelis
articles.summary: A new government would not end the occupation, but it could rein in the far right and ease tensions across the region.
articles.body:
In Israel’s convoluted political discourse, just days before a general election that many regard as one of the most consequential in the country’s history, the prevailing perception is that the current coalition and the opposition parties are running neck and neck.

This is far from the full picture. Most polls suggest that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his far-right and ultra-Orthodox partners will fall short of a parliamentary majority. Most opposition parties, at least until the last polling station closes and the final results become known, have ruled out forming a coalition government with the parties that primarily represent Israel’s Palestinian citizens, commonly referred to as the “Arab parties”. As a result, the opposition could also struggle to secure the support needed to govern.

If the opinion polls prove accurate on Tuesday and the opposition can overcome this obstacle to forming a governing majority, a new government could emerge, led by retired Lieutenant General Gadi Eisenkot, a former Israeli military chief of staff from the centre right.

However, the fundamental question is not simply whether the Israeli electorate will decide to change the personnel in government but whether the new leadership will also bring about a change in policy on the most crucial issues facing the country and, by extension, the Palestinians and the wider region. My answer is yes but with significant qualifications.

After a total of nearly two decades in power over the past three decades, including the last four years at the helm of what has arguably been the most far-right and inept government in Israel’s history, Netanyahu may leave behind a deeply scarred country. His determination to retain power has come at the cost of national cohesion, exacerbating fear and a profound siege mentality in Israeli society.

Throughout his time in office, Netanyahu has cynically exploited and manipulated this deeply ingrained sense of insecurity. The horrific Hamas-led October 7 attacks aggravated these fears, pushing Israeli politics further to the right. Most opposition parties are themselves centre-right or right-wing, but they differ considerably from the parties that currently make up the governing coalition.

To begin with, Netanyahu’s decisions on the most fundamental issues facing the country, including national security, have been distorted by the extraordinary circumstances of his standing trial in three corruption cases on charges of fraud, breach of trust and bribery. Consequently, he was prepared first to legitimise and bolster the messianic far right, helping to make its representatives politically acceptable, and then to form a coalition with them.

Other politicians were unwilling to serve under a prime minister facing such charges alongside these extreme national-chauvinistic parties. Eisenkot and Benny Gantz did join an emergency government led by Netanyahu after the October 7 attacks, but left once they realised he was caving in to the far right.

A new prime minister, unencumbered by these personal legal considerations, would have greater freedom to govern without the overriding motive of remaining in power at any cost to avoid accountability in his own corruption cases.

One can argue with a high degree of confidence that a different Israeli government three years ago would have conducted the war in Gaza very differently and agreed to a ceasefire much earlier, facilitating the release of the hostages and sparing many thousands of innocent Palestinian lives. A government without Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich would also be more likely to cooperate with United States President Donald Trump’s peace plan and the Board of Peace.

At least in the short term, this could improve humanitarian conditions in the Gaza Strip and pave the way towards some degree of an Israeli withdrawal, even if an immediate and complete withdrawal remains unlikely.

The government that might emerge from the opposition parties, while far from my ideal, could serve as a government of containment – akin to the fictional “little Dutch boy” who plugged a hole in a dike with his finger to prevent a catastrophic flood. Such a government would be unlikely to hesitate to halt and reverse the so-called judicial overhaul, which amounted to an assault on the separation of powers, the system of checks and balances, and, for all intents and purposes, the democratic system itself.

Another Netanyahu-Ben-Gvir government would risk leaving Israel a democracy in name only, with serious consequences not only for its domestic affairs but also for worsening oppression in the occupied Palestinian territory and for its foreign relations.

For instance, a government different from the current one would be unlikely to entertain proposals, heard from the coalition benches, to abolish the Jewish Division of the Shin Bet, Israel’s internal security and counterintelligence service. Without this division, settler terrorist violence would be likely to increase further and continue with near-total impunity.

A new government would also be more likely to base appointments to senior civil service positions on merit rather than political affiliation or personal loyalty to the prime minister, as is often the case under the current government. Moreover, the opposition parties would be expected to honour their promise to take decisive action against terrorist attacks on innocent Palestinians. These attacks have intensified during the olive harvest, making a prompt and sustained response all the more urgent.

Another area in which such a government could make a difference is the approved E1 settlement project, for which construction tenders have already been issued. Whether motivated by ideological considerations, strategic concerns or a desire to ease tensions with the international community, suspending or cancelling the project could be an important first step towards containing settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank.

It is not unrealistic to assume that a new government might adopt an approach that relies less exclusively on military force in Lebanon and Syria and possibly in relation to Iran while remaining open to exploring diplomatic avenues. It would also be less likely to engage in the constant political theatre designed to appease a far-right, ultranationalist base – as the current government has done by passing a law introducing the death penalty for Palestinians convicted of certain terrorist offences and proposing to surround prisons holding Palestinian security prisoners with crocodiles.

You might think that this is an exceptionally low benchmark. Indeed, Eisenkot himself opposes Palestinian statehood and favours continued Israeli security control over Palestinian territory while the opposition’s refusal to work with Arab parties underscores the limits of the change it offers. Yet, under the current circumstances, changing the political discourse and restoring a degree of normality to domestic debate and to Israel’s relations with its regional and international partners could make a real difference. It could, in time, open the way to more rapid and transformative change, provided the international community remains actively and constructively engaged.

At times like these, recognising that politics is the art of the possible and holding a new government accountable for the direction and pace of its promised changes, with a clear sense of urgency, could yield positive results. But first, the electorate must give this possibility a chance at the ballot box.

articles.title: Private Parking Code of Practice: Will it end 'rip-off' charges?
articles.summary: The prime minister says a new code will end "rip-off parking charges" - but will it work?
articles.body:
"I was completely on edge, every single day," said Rosey Greenwood. "I had letters coming through - I had debt collectors after me."

Two years ago, Rosey was being told to pay £1,906 because she had taken too long to pay for parking.

Rosey had paid every single time she parked at the Copeland Street car park in Derby, and had bank records to prove it. But Rosey had unknowingly broken the car park's terms and conditions, which stipulated that drivers must pay within five minutes of entering.

Rosey could not afford to pay £1,906 - she was due to get married and also saving up to buy her first home.

As she prepared to fight the case in court, her fiance emailed the BBC and asked us to "shed some light" on what was happening .

The case was then raised in Parliament by Derby North MP Catherine Atkinson, who described the charges - which had caught out countless other motorists - as a "five-minute rip-off charge".

The parking sector subsequently banned the five-minute payment rule by updating its code of practice , but the government is going further by bringing in a statutory Private Parking Code of Practice.

"These charges leave people feeling ripped off and out of pocket, so I'm putting a stop to them," Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Monday.

But will the new code actually put the brakes on "rip-off" parking charges?

The government's new Private Parking Code of Practice was laid out in Parliament on Tuesday.

It sets out standards that parking operators must follow.

Housing and communities minister Florence Eshalomi said the new code "will give drivers a range of rights and protections to make these unfair practices a thing of the past".

The code is now subject to a 40-day period of parliamentary scrutiny, during which MPs and peers can object before it is formally issued.

The code will then come into force 21 calendar days from the point of issue.

In places, the code appears to be very similar to the private parking sector's existing code of practice .

For example, Eshalomi said drivers would "now have a guaranteed minimum five minutes to decide whether to park", known as the consideration period.

However, the sector's code already gives drivers a minimum consideration period of five minutes, so this does not appear to be new.

The government's code also gives drivers a 10-minute grace period in which to leave a car park following the end of their permitted stay.

However, the sector's code already gives drivers a 10-minute grace period, so this does not appear to be new either.

The government's code sets the maximum parking charge at £100, or £60 if paid within a fortnight. This is also the same as in the sector's code.

The government's code states charges should be reduced to £20 on appeal under four circumstances: not displaying a parking permit despite having a valid one, entering the wrong vehicle registration into a parking machine, not entering a registration at all, and not displaying a Blue Badge despite having one.

The sector's code already said charges should be reduced to £20 under those circumstances.

Parking operators will also still be allowed to add a £70 debt recovery fee to each parking charge if drivers do not pay, as well as court fees and legal costs.

The government code states parking charges should be cancelled on appeal where the driver or a passenger in the vehicle suffers the onset of illness, where the driver or a passenger is delayed by an overrunning medical appointment, where the driver suffers delays due to childcare arrangements, and where a vehicle is broken down.

In contrast, the sector's code said these charges should be reduced to £20.

The government's code says parking operators who do not comply will lose access to DVLA vehicle keeper data, meaning they will no longer be able to issue parking charges.

This is meant to happen already, because parking operators need to be members of one of two trade associations in order to access DVLA data, and they can theoretically lose their membership if they break the rules.

Campaigners claim this has not happened in practice, but the government insists it will happen in future.

There will also be what the government describes as a "fully independent Scrutiny and Oversight Board".

Jack Cousens, head of roads policy at the AA, said the benefit of the new code was that it was backed by the government, rather than the parking sector itself.

"That means, if there are any changes to be made, it will come via the government and indeed via the independent scrutiny panel," he added.

"Up until now, the private industry have held the pen on changing the code of practice. Now the pen is firmly in the hand of the government."

Both the AA and RAC have welcomed the statutory code of practice - which they campaigned for - but believe it does not go far enough.

For example, the AA believes there needs to be a single and independent appeals process.

"Drivers need to have confidence that when they are making their representations, it's being heard by an independent body, as opposed to the private parking operators and their trade bodies marking their own homework," Cousens said.

The AA also believes the government needs to find an alternative to debt recovery fees and charges, which often "spiral" into the threat of court action and County Court Judgments.

This was how Rosey was asked to pay a total of £1,906 for 10 parking charges, and also how Hannah Robinson was asked to pay £11,390 .

"We've long called for the banning of debt recovery fees being added on top of parking charge notices, and a single independent appeals body to replace the two industry-run ones, but neither have been included [in the code] which is disappointing," head of policy Simon Williams said.

The government said it was "consulting as soon as possible next year on private parking debt recovery fees, including on whether to cut an existing £70 cap or scrap the fees altogether".

Parking campaigner Lynda Eagan, who helped Rosey, is sceptical about how much has changed.

"I've been screaming at the TV every time I see someone saying 'we've got these new things'," she said.

"They've tweaked a few things here and there, but it's not actually going to make an awful lot of difference to people.

"How, when not much has really changed, is that going to reduce the number of PCNs [parking charge notices]?"

In response, a Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government spokesperson said: "We don't accept these claims. We've introduced a new Private Parking Code of Practice that will have statutory force and independent oversight.

"We've introduced significant changes to make life fairer for drivers, including cancelling the £20 charge for circumstances outside a someone's control like an overrunning medical appointment, and helping motorists get a fairer outcome with strengthened requirements for appeals."

One thing Eagan is looking forward to is the new oversight board , although she is concerned it will not be truly independent.

"We are hopeful that it could make some difference to some drivers, and we hope that it stops some of the more spurious claims being stopped at source, but we will be watching," Cousens said.

The two trade associations for parking operators, which wrote the sector's existing code, are reading and reviewing the government's changes.

Alison Tooze, chief policy officer at the British Parking Association, said: "Overall, the code strikes the right balance between stronger protections for motorists and effective parking management, helping keep communities, businesses and local economies moving."

She said retaining a £100 parking charge was important.

"Evidence shows that meaningful deterrents support compliance and good behaviours, helping ensure parking remains available for those who need it and enabling parking to be managed effectively," she added.

A spokesperson for the International Parking Community (IPC) said: "The IPC has long supported a code that raises standards, and we are now reviewing it in detail to understand what it means for motorists, landowners and operators alike.

"Any changes must remain fair to motorists while staying workable, so that compliant motorists are not disadvantaged by those who choose to ignore the rules."

The £1,906 court claim against Rosey was dropped following publicity about the case. She has since married her fiance and they have bought a house together.

She is hopeful the new code will prevent other people going through what she did.

"I feel like our voices have been heard; fellow motorists like myself have been listened to," she said.

"I hope that in the future people won't be so worried or fearful of going into car parks like the one I went to."

articles.title: Firms in Devon 'holding back' on new jobs ahead of Budget
articles.summary: Some businesses say they want to see employment costs come down in the October Budget.
articles.body:
Some businesses are calling for the costs of employing staff to be brought down in the Budget on Wednesday.

A publisher from Tavistock, Devon, said he was "holding back" from filling two new positions at his firm because of the cost of taking on new employees.

At the Devon Business Show some firms said they had been struggling for the past two years to deal with the increases in employers' National Insurance contributions introduced in 2024, while also coping with increases in the National Minimum Wage .

Chancellor John Healey will deliver his first Budget on Wednesday but has refused to rule out tax increases after acknowledging government borrowing costs are at "historic highs".

Michelle Bunker, from WGP Maintenance, in Plymouth, said she had one clear message for the chancellor: "I want to see National Insurance contributions starting to go down."

Tim Randell, who runs Links Publishing, said changes to government policy would allow him to employ more people.

He said: "All we've had for the last two Budgets is more tax, more expense, the living wage, and all those things mean that people like me are not employing the young.

"I have two positions that I could fill, want to fill, want to expand and grow my business, but I'm holding back because of the employment costs."

In the 2024 Budget, Rachel Reeves announced companies would have to pay National Insurance at 15% on salaries above £5,000 from April 2025, up from 13.8% on salaries above £9,100.

The legal minimum wage for over-21s also rose from £11.44 to £12.21 per hour from April 2025.

Kevin Miller, the boss of Apex HR, in Plymouth, said small businesses were "the backbone of the whole economy" and needed help.

He said: "We need to reduce the cost of employing people because we're all passionate about really wanting to build this economy and grow it - so help us out with some tax relief please..."

The cost of living crisis is affecting charities as much as businesses, according to Elsbeth Hallam, from Plymouth-based Hugs Children's Cancer Charity, which supports families with children with cancer.

She said: "People are definitely being tighter on what they're spending their money on.

"For us, obviously it does have a run-on effect then on what we can raise and how many families we can support."

Tens of thousands of people are employed in hospitality and catering in Devon and hotel bosses said the industry had been going through a tough time.

People working in hospitality - spearheaded by celebrity chef Tom Kerridge - have long been campaigning for a reduction in VAT for pubs and restaurants from 20% to 10% .

Melanie Williams, events manager at the Duke of Cornwall Hotel, in Plymouth, said: "I think people's financial pockets are strained and any support we can be given from the government within the budget has got to benefit everybody in the industry - VAT perhaps to be revisited again."

Pete Adams, general manager at the Moxy Hotel, in Plymouth, joined the call for a cut to VAT for the hospitality sector.

He said: "That would allow us to pass some of those savings on to the customer.

"That will then hopefully increase more customers into our businesses and extra spending and that'll give the Treasury almost as much money as before."

The Devon Business Show was hosted by Devon Chamber of Commerce at the Plymouth Life Centre.

Helen Wylde-Archibald, CEO of Devon Chamber of Commerce, said businesses in the county were "planning for a better future".

She said: "I think what we just need is that soft touch with the Budget so that businesses get the chance to grow and I think Devon will be right at the front of the pack."

The government insisted it was "on the side of business" and said easing the cost of doing business was one of the chancellor's five priorities.

A spokesperson for HM Treasury said: "The chancellor is giving firms the breathing space to invest and grow, with business rates cuts, a cap on corporation tax, £4.3 billion of support to limit bill rises, and employer National Insurance contributions relief when hiring under-21s and apprentices under 25.

"As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the chancellor to set out at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals."

articles.title: Sisters buy five model lighthouses to remember loved ones
articles.summary: Family spends almost £14,000 on lighthouses saying it is the perfect way to support hospice charity.
articles.body:
A family have bought a chain of lighthouse models in memory of loved ones and to thank the hospice charity which cared for them.

Sisters Kim Hill and Nicola Oliver bought the models which were sold at auction at the end of St Luke's Hospice Plymouth's Guiding Lights trail .

The women said they were inspired to buy the lighthouses because of their personal experiences with the charity.

Their mother was cared for at the hospice specialist unit in 2024 and Hill's husband Brian was looked after by St Luke's nursing teams before he died in June this year.

Between them the sisters spent almost £14,000 on the lighthouses but Hill said the auction was an easy way to give the charity a "large sum on money" because it wouldn't have occurred to her to make a donation of that size.

"You hope you're never going to have to use the facility again but if you do it's there and it's worth supporting to make sure it remains there," she said.

The 42 lighthouses making up the trail were unveiled at an exhibition in July before being moved to locations around Plymouth.

Hill said she had hoped to complete the lighthouse trail with her husband but they did not have the chance.

"Sadly he passed away before the (lighthouse) trail started but he did know that at the end of it they were going to auction the lighthouses off and he knew I wanted to buy one," she said.

Forty-two big lighthouses were designed and decorated by artists, while a further 42 little lighthouses, designed by schools, were displayed at the Box Gallery and Museum, and another 10 sculptures toured venues across Devon.

Hill said she had an auction brochure and put stars against the ones she wanted to bid on.

"We did have a plan B of maybe we'll get one between us. But we didn't need plan B, our plan A worked."

In the end she bought three lighthouses at the auction - Light of Plymouth for £4,200, Mega Murals for £2,800 and Devon Delights for £2,600. A total of £9,600.

"I wanted ones that were connected to Plymouth," said Hill.

"My husband was Scottish, but he loved the city. He was in the Royal Navy and lived here since 1977 or 78. We were together 46 years. He would approve of me buying the lighthouses, I'm sure," she said.

The Light of Plymouth lighthouse lives in Hill's back garden but the others have found permanent homes with family members.

Mega Murals was bought for her daughter and Devon Delights went to her son and daughter in law who no longer live in Devon.

"It's their piece of Devon shipped to Worcester," she said.

Oliver said her son, who has a disability, loved the trail so much he visited each lighthouse several times, going on two or three expeditions a week over the summer and was very keen to have one to keep.

She placed winning bids on two lighthouses including Walkies! for £2,000, which is covered in dogs and now lives in her front garden, and Just Keep Swimming, for £2,200, which has a new home in her back garden by her swimming pool. A total of £4,200.

"The trail has been lovely," said Nicola. "As they appeared in Plymouth they were so magnificent."

She added she felt it was "enlightening" at the auction to hear about the costs the charity face.

"In the times that we've used them there's never been any emphasis from them on how much it costs," she said.

She said it was "a really nice feeling" to know other people would be helped because of the money they had spent on the lighthouses.

Hill added: "At the worst time in your life, you know, the care is there.

"It's a brilliant facility on our doorstep, you never hope you're going to have to go there but our mum went there twice and it was the best care," she said.

She added: "My husband didn't want to go to St Luke's, but the St Luke's ladies cared for him at home for the last three weeks of his life.

"Very cheery ladies doing a difficult job at a very difficult time, very supportive to myself and they were willing to show me how to help care for him."

Penny Hannah, St Luke's head of fundraising, said the project had been "absolutely magical".

She added: "The money raised at auction is enough to make a difference for more than 200 families in our community when they desperately need the expert care and support we provide."

articles.title: How families are cutting the cost of Halloween as spending grows
articles.summary: Families are turning to homemade costumes, swaps and second-hand outfits to keep it affordable.
articles.body:
Halloween has become one of the UK's biggest seasonal celebrations, with spending on costumes, decorations and themed events continuing to grow.

As a mum, I have already found myself buying three costumes for different Halloween occasions this year. For many families, the costs can add up quickly.

That is why some parents say they are increasingly turning to costume swaps, second-hand outfits and homemade creations rather than buying new every year.

Earlier this month, businesses told the BBC that Halloween had become more important than Christmas for some attractions and retailers, while a survey found 36% of shoppers planned to celebrate Halloween this year, up from 27% in 2025.

From Facebook groups dedicated to swapping outfits to charity shop bargains and creative upcycling projects, families are finding ways to embrace the spooky season without frightening their finances.

For Birmingham mum Mandy Thomas, finding affordable costumes became essential when her daughters were younger.

"I figured out really quickly that I needed to cut costs where I could when Halloween came around," she said.

"There would be a school event, trick-or-treating and a friend's party, and they didn't want to dress up as the same thing every time.

"A friend put me onto these Facebook groups where people swap or sell costumes really cheaply.

"When one of them wants to be a specific character, I search eBay or Vinted and I usually spend a quarter of the original price."

With many costumes worn only a handful of times before being packed away, swapping and reselling outfits has become a popular way for parents to save money while helping to reduce waste.

Charity shops have also noticed increased demand for Halloween outfits.

At the RSPCA charity shop in Coundon, Coventry, manager Ellya Hayden said staff prepare for the spooky season throughout the year by putting aside suitable donations.

"We know that at Halloween and Christmas there's going to be lots of buying going on, and people prefer to cut costs by shopping in charity shops," she said.

"We save any sellable costumes that come in and get them ready for display.

"It's really great to see the kids coming in and getting excited and there's always someone who needs a last-minute costume."

Some costumes sell for as little as £1.50, she said, while items still in their original packaging are often priced at about a quarter of their retail value.

"It's really important to reuse and recycle costumes. We try to repair items where we can so they can have multiple lives," Hayden said.

For some families, saving money means making something from scratch.

In Coventry, Adele Harrison, founder of not-for-profit organisation Cov Cloth, runs workshops that teach children and parents how to transform unwanted textiles and household items into Halloween costumes, decorations and accessories.

She said the sessions help families develop creative habits while showing that many Halloween outfits can be made using items already found at home.

"Our Halloween workshops are especially popular," she said.

"Young people have a great day and leave with homemade Halloween treasures, including accessories, costumes and decorations they've made themselves."

Although families pay to attend the sessions, Harrison said the principles could easily be applied using old tights, cereal boxes and unwanted clothing.

"Our message is: before heading to the shops, use what you already have," she said.

"Get creative, save some money and let your children see how brilliant they are.

"The families may not necessarily see it as a money-saver on the day, but the practices we promote are money-saving creative habits."

articles.title: Man spits gutkha from 3rd-floor balcony, dies after coming in contact with 11kV wire
articles.summary: BHOPAL: Spitting gutkha from his third-floor balcony may have cost a 65-year-old man his life after he reportedly came in contact with an 11kV
articles.body: BHOPAL: Spitting gutkha from his third-floor balcony may have cost a 65-year-old man his life after he reportedly came in contact with an 11kV high-tension power line in Ganjbasoda, in Madhya Pradesh’s Vidisha district, on Friday afternoon.Prabhulal Gupta was standing on the balcony of his rented house in Gayatri Nagar around 1pm when the incident occurred. According to local residents, the stream of saliva he spat while chewing gutkha came in contact with the overhead wire, leaving him severely burnt.Gupta, a mason originally from Chhatarpur, had been living in the rented house for the past 10 years.Electrical experts said such an incident could occur under certain conditions. Saliva contains moisture and dissolved salts, which can make it conductive. If a continuous stream of fluid reached a live conductor, it could potentially provide a conductive path for electricity.Experts also said an 11kV line could produce an electrical arc under suitable conditions. If the balcony was sufficiently close to the conductor, electricity could jump through the air. If an electrical path through the body was established, the resulting shock could cause severe burns or death.The incident triggered anger among residents, who alleged that the electricity company had ignored repeated complaints about high-tension wires passing dangerously close to houses.One of Gupta’s landlords said electricity poles, wires and distribution transformers in the locality were in poor condition. Residents had repeatedly complained about the 11kV line passing close to homes, but their concerns had not been addressed.Landlord Padma Chidhar said she had also approached electricity officials several times, seeking the removal of the line. articles.title: Jersey Museum's interactive light event showcases island life
articles.summary: The museum says the exhibition will look at the history of light and its uses in Jersey.
articles.body:
A laser harp which uses light to play music, and a shadow-freezing photo booth are both part of an exhibition celebrating the science of light.

Jersey Museum's interactive event opened on Saturday at Jersey Museum and explores how "light has been used in Jersey over the years".

It said Playing with Light explored how light had helped to "tell the time, light our homes, safely guide shipping and entertain us".

Lucy Layton, Jersey Heritage exhibitions curator, said the event promised to be "one of the most fun" exhibitions in the museum's history.

Layton said the exhibition, called Jouer auve la Leunmiéthe in Jèrriais - the island's native language - would feature "lots of ways to play with light".

These, she said, included "buttons and levers", that helped visitors discover more about rainbows, lighthouses, and Jersey's role in early photography.

Photos of August's eclipse are also included, the museum said.

Collection items included coloured glassware, Victorian chemist shop bottles, an 18th Century sundial, and a homemade dynamo torch from the Occupation years.

The exhibition will be open until the end of December, and is suitable for children aged six and older. Museum admission prices apply.

articles.title: Israel to close occupied West Bank crossings as it locks down Hebron
articles.summary: Israel says it will close all land crossings with the West Bank when it holds a general election on Tuesday.
articles.body:
Israel says it will close all land crossings with the occupied West Bank on the day of its general election this coming week.

The Israeli army said in a statement on Sunday that it would bar Palestinian workers from entering most areas of the West Bank from Sunday through Monday and enforce a full closure of crossings into and out of the territory on Tuesday, the day of the vote.

The announcement comes a day after the Israeli army imposed a lockdown in Hebron and forced thousands of Palestinians from their homes.

It has conducted hundreds of raids since Friday’s attack in the city by two Palestinian gunmen on an Israeli army reserve base, which killed two Israeli soldiers. The two Palestinians were also killed.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordered a “full lockdown” of the West Bank after the attack while Defence Minister Israel Katz confirmed “about 2,000” people had been forcibly displaced.

“They will not be allowed to return to their neighbourhood until we’ve finished dealing with all the Hamas issues in Hebron,” Katz said in an interview with the public broadcaster Kan.

Hebron Mayor Yousef al-Ja’bari told Al Jazeera that the city and several neighbouring villages were under a complete blockade.

He also said on Saturday that 2,200 people had been forced from their homes by Israeli soldiers and raids.

The Palestinian Authority (PA), which governs parts of Hebron and the West Bank, has called for international pressure on Israel to protect Hebron’s residents, who said soldiers announced forced evacuation orders over loudspeakers late at night, leaving them with no time to prepare and few places to go.

The PA called Israel’s actions “collective punishment”, citing the demolition of homes, forced displacement of entire neighbourhoods, and the “closure and siege of Palestinian cities”.

About 200,000 Palestinians live in the city of Hebron and a further 600,000 in Hebron governorate, making it the West Bank’s most populous area.

The Israeli military has said the operation will last several days.

But Netanyahu suggested bigger action was coming, saying he was planning an operation on a scale not seen since Israel occupied the West Bank in 1967.

Netanyahu, Israel’s longest serving prime minister, is facing a tight race in Tuesday’s elections, and analysts said he is trying to capitalise on ongoing regional military conflicts and national security fears to anchor his re-election campaign.

articles.title: Kansas woman says she agreed to buy her cousin’s home on about 5 acres after curing a $9,055 mortgage default; four years later he received a $150,000 offer, but an appeals court enforced their oral deal
articles.summary: A Kansas man who received a $150,000 offer for his property has lost a legal battle with his cousin, who claimed he had already agreed to sell her the
articles.body: A Kansas man who received a $150,000 offer for his property has lost a legal battle with his cousin, who claimed he had already agreed to sell her the house and about five acres of land four years earlier. Tiffany Miller said she took responsibility for the property in 2020 after discovering that her cousin, Aaron Harvey, had fallen behind on mortgage payments. Although they never signed a sale agreement, the Kansas Court of Appeals ruled on Friday that their verbal arrangement could be enforced.The dispute began when Harvey decided to sell the property in 2024. By then, Miller and her son had been paying the mortgage and looking after the house for several years. They had also spent money repairing the building and improving the surrounding land. Harvey, however, maintained that he had never agreed to sell it to them.According to the court ruling available on Justia, the disagreement came to a head in March 2024, when Miller noticed a sale sign outside the Kansas City property. Harvey later told the court that he had received a $150,000 offer from another buyer, who had also provided a cashier's cheque. At the time of the trial, around $49,000 remained outstanding on the mortgage.How a mortgage problem led to the agreementHarvey had owned the property since 2004. He had previously lived there and borrowed $75,000 in 2005 to renovate the house and build an arena for cattle roping. Miller was familiar with the land because her son, Demetre, kept horses there.In January 2020, while visiting to feed the horses, Miller came across a letter addressed to Harvey. She testified that it warned the property was at risk of foreclosure and that $9,055.68 was needed to bring the mortgage payments up to date.Miller contacted Harvey about the letter and said he indicated that he no longer wanted the property. She then offered to buy it.According to Miller, they agreed on a price of $80,000. With approximately $61,000 still owed on the mortgage, she would take responsibility for the loan and pay Harvey the remaining $19,000 by January 1, 2025. He would then transfer ownership to her.The overdue mortgage amount was not paid as a single upfront payment. Instead, Miller arranged a modification of the loan, which added the overdue amount to the mortgage balance. The lender approved the arrangement in May 2020.Harvey gave a different account. He said he had simply allowed Miller's family to use the property in exchange for paying the mortgage and utility bills. He denied agreeing to sell it.Years of repairs became important to the caseThe condition of the house became an important part of the dispute. Miller testified that when she first received the keys in January 2020, she found mud, mould and mildew in the basement, along with a sewer smell. When she told Harvey about the problems, she said he responded, "That's your deal now."Miller and her son subsequently carried out extensive work. They repaired plumbing, replaced household appliances, improved fencing and worked on the driveway and cattle arena. They also installed a French drain to prevent water from entering the basement. Her son began contributing towards the mortgage, utilities and repairs after moving into the property in 2022.Harvey argued that he had not been informed about the improvements. However, the trial court found that his actions supported Miller's account, particularly because he had given her access to the mortgage account and allowed her to take possession of the property.Why court rejected Harvey's appealHarvey argued that the original arrangement was unfair because the property had subsequently attracted a $150,000 offer. He pointed out that Miller would pay him only $19,000 directly, even though the property's value had increased considerably.The appeals court disagreed with that comparison. The judges explained that the agreed purchase price was $80,000, including the mortgage Miller had undertaken to pay. They also considered the repairs and improvements made over the years.Another issue involved Miller's bankruptcy filing in 2022. She admitted that she had not disclosed the property agreement or mortgage payments, describing the omission as an "honest mistake". Harvey argued that this should prevent her from claiming the property, but the appeals court found that he had not properly raised that defence during the earlier proceedings.The judges also considered whether an agreement that was never written down could still be enforced. Although Kansas law generally requires property-sale agreements to be in writing, exceptions can apply when someone has already acted substantially on an agreement.In this case, the court found sufficient evidence that Miller had acted on the arrangement by taking possession, arranging the mortgage payments and making significant improvements.The judges also concluded that simply paying her back for the repairs would not adequately compensate her for losing the property she had agreed to buy.You use AI every day.
