articles.title: Online trend driving urban explorer break-ins, estate owner says
articles.summary: A video filmed inside cottages near Leadenham House is blamed for sparking "copycat" incidents.
articles.body:
The owner of a Georgian country house believes "online trends" have driven break-ins at his properties.

William Reeve, who owns Leadenham House, Lincolnshire, said a video posted on social media showing an "urban explorer" inside one of his cottages, sparked "copycat" incidents, including intruders entering his home while he slept.

Dr Kevin Bingham, an expert on urban exploring, said social media was leading some people to take it up "for the wrong reasons now and not for genuine interest in historical sites".

Lincolnshire Police said it had received three reports from the area since 11 October, including suspicious activity, a break-in at a property awaiting renovation and a burglary.

A video filmed inside cottages, which Reeve owns and said he had left locked, was posted on social media on 7 October and attracted more than 60,000 views.

He said the cottages, which are due to be refurbished, subsequently became the target of repeat trespassing by people attempting to find the locations featured in the video.

He added that four intruders then broke into his home while he was sleeping on 18 October.

"I felt immediately violated, furious and anxious," Reeve said.

"People see the video and think it's alright to go into the property. Suddenly it becomes acceptable.

"They break in, access it and call it abandoned."

Police said in the incident on 18 October, damage was caused to antique furniture, gates and a padlock, while an adjacent workshop was also broken into.

Urban exploring involves visiting and documenting abandoned, disused or rarely accessed places. This can involve trespassing, a civil matter.

However, breaking into buildings and causing damage are criminal offences.

Reeve said: "This social media trend has more ramifications than just innocent urban exploring.

"They've graduated from trespassing to breaking and entering."

Bingham, from the University of Lincoln, said social media had driven an increase in the popularity of urban exploring and "changed" it for some participants.

"What was once a niche activity, largely confined to specialist forums, is now being shared with far wider audiences on mainstream social media platforms.

"We've gone from the saying 'leave only footprints' and 'take only photographs' to a free for all.

"People think they can chop off the lock, get in there and get the content."

Bingham, the author of An Ethnography of Urban Exploration, stressed that most urban explorers were respectful.

"It's the individuals that are willing to break in and smash windows that give it a really bad name."

Zoe Angeloni, who lives in a cottage nearby, said she was disturbed by urban explorers during the incident on 18 October.

Police said five people were spotted going in and out of one empty property and running away from another, which was occupied.

Angeloni said her husband had gone outside to investigate and had torches shone into his eyes before a group of people had run off.

"It's not just breaking into these properties, it's having a knock-on impact on the community as well," Angeloni said.

Police said inquiries and footage from the incidents had offered insufficient evidence to identify those responsible.

Urban exploring content is popular across social media platforms.

According to TikTok – the platform on which the original video was posted on 7 October – the account behind it was subsequently removed for breaching community guidelines, which include not showing or promoting crime. The BBC attempted to contact the owner of the account.

One experienced urban explorer said the alleged incidents at Leadenham House did not reflect the approach of the wider exploring community.

Alistair, who is part of a YouTube channel called Urbandoned, said urban exploring should focus on documenting the history of genuine abandoned sites, rather than chasing online attention.

"We genuinely just love exploring abandoned buildings and documenting them," he said.

"We try to do it in a serious, professional and historical way."

He said members of his group would "never break into any building", adding: "It's not the right way to do it, it's morally wrong."

Social media had changed the landscape of urban exploring, with some people more interested in gaining "hits and views" than in the history of the building, he added.

"As the scene has got so popular, there are more people willing to break in and not care about the consequences."

Lincolnshire Police said it always advised people never to enter abandoned or derelict buildings, which were often unsafe and could result in serious injury.

articles.title: Israeli forces turn Hebron homes into military posts amid lockdown
articles.summary: Evictions, raids and outpost expansion continue across the occupied West Bank amid heightened tensions.
articles.body:
Israeli forces have turned Palestinian homes in the city of Hebron into barracks and observation posts after forcing residents to leave, as a military operation in the southern occupied West Bank continues, the Palestinian news agency Wafa has reported.

They took over homes in the Khallat Manna and Dahiyat al-Zaytoun areas of southern Hebron to use them as barracks, and forced residents from homes in other neighbourhoods to use the properties as observation posts, Wafa said, citing sources.

The Israeli military has imposed a lockdown in Hebron and conducted hundreds of raids since two armed Palestinian men allegedly carried out an attack on an Israeli army reserve base on Friday, killing two soldiers. The two suspects were also killed.

The evictions follow the forced displacement of hundreds of families amid extensive raids, road closures and tight restrictions on movement.

According to the Palestinian Prisoner’s Society, Israeli forces have detained at least 47 Palestinians across Hebron since Friday, while forcibly displacing 293 families, comprising about 2,200 people.

Among those displaced from Hebron are 127 infants, 81 pregnant women and 26 people with disabilities, the NGO told Al Jazeera. The displaced also include 134 Palestinians with chronic illnesses and 265 elderly people over the age of 60.

Israeli troops also conducted hundreds of field interrogations, subjecting Palestinians to detention and abuse, the group said.

Meanwhile, Israeli settlers began establishing two new outposts on Palestinian-owned land in the town of Yatta, south of Hebron, Wafa reported.

Activist Osama Makhamra told Wafa that settlers began setting up an outpost in the Khallet al-Fara area, west of Yatta, where they pitched a tent, brought in bulldozers and excavation machinery, and started levelling and digging the land in preparation for construction.

He added that another outpost was established in the Yatta desert area, on Palestinian-owned land between the villages of az-Zuweidin and Umm Qussa, where settlers pitched several tents and began installing infrastructure, including water and electricity networks.

Near Bethlehem, Israeli forces continued to close roads and entrances across the governorate for the third consecutive day on Sunday, affecting several towns and villages, Wafa reported.

On Saturday, Israeli forces shut down dirt roads leading to Tuqu to block access, firing tear gas canisters and stun grenades towards Palestinian vehicles travelling along rough alternative routes near the town.

The latest attacks and closures come days before Israel’s general elections and as tensions remain high across the occupied Palestinian territory, where settlers, backed by the military, have carried out a wave of pogroms targeting olive harvesters .

articles.title: Thousands in North West without power and cars wrecked in Storm Boelo
articles.summary: Thousands are without power and 400 people are evacuated from a caravan park in Preston.
articles.body:
Storm Boelo has uprooted trees which have smashed into cars and left tens of thousands of people without powers as it blows across the North West.

SP Electricity North West said thousands of homes had been hit by power cuts caused by strong gust of winds, with more than 500 homes affected in Blackpool and 200 in Wigan alone.

More than 400 people had to be evacuated from a caravan park near Preston, Lancashire, and a family day race meeting at Merseyside's Aintree racecourse has been cancelled.

Grandmother Lisa Roberts said she had been left in tears after a tree fell on her car in Heysham, Lancashire.

Roberts told BBC Radio Lancashire: "We had just sat down to watch Strictly - there was a lot of noise outside but you expect that when it's windy.

"But suddenly there was an almighty noise and my husband went out and said 'it's a tree - it's landed on the car'.

"It smashed through the sunroof and the windscreen.

"It's not what we expected on a Saturday night [but] my five-year-old grandson did predict it.

"He said earlier 'look at that tree nana - it's going to fall over'."

Aintree racecourse said its Halloween Fun Day had been "abandoned due to high winds" after it reported gusts of up to 44mph.

In a statement, it said: "While we are disappointed, the safety of our participants, visitors and teams is our number one priority."

Bates pumpkin farm in Warrington, Cheshire, also announced it had shut for the day as the "50mph gusts are not safe to be on the farm".

Visit Liverpool announced its River of Light event, featuring illuminated artworks, had been cancelled "in the interests of safety".

Gusts of more than 70mph have been experienced in many areas and large waves have battered the coast.

The Met Office said Storm Boelo could bring a danger to life from flying debris and crashing waves and people should stay indoors as much as possible.

Trams have been cancelled in Blackpool due to heavy rain and high winds, while Avanti West Coast has advised people not to travel north of Preston.

TransPennine Express said a tree fell on the line between Liverpool Lime Street and Manchester Piccadilly, causing major delays.

articles.title: The penguins are noisy, the people fantastic - what it takes to be an Antarctic postmaster
articles.summary: George Clarke from Bristol will run the post office at Port Lockroy in Antarctica from October to March.
articles.body:
It is hardly a typical round for a postie, but for five months of the year George Clarke leaves behind his partner and friends in Bristol to become a postmaster at the world's most southerly post office - in Antarctica.

"I thought it sounded like an amazing experience - living away from home for a few months on a very small island with five other people and 1,000 penguins," says Clarke.

He takes up his role as Port Lockroy postmaster from late October to March, during the southern hemisphere summer.

The part-time festival worker and artist says his days are spent sorting postcards, processing letters and arranging for the post to hitch a ride north on passing ships before being distributed around the world.

"The penguins are noisy and smelly. The people are fantastic," he said. "I've fallen in love with the Antarctic wilderness."

When Clarke sets off with in a team of six on Monday, it will be his third voyage to Antarctica helping the UK Antarctic Heritage Trust (UKAHT) to conserve Port Lockroy, a former British science research facility.

Unlike a regular post office, there is no fleet of vans ready to whisk the mail away.

"When we collect up all the postcards and we've sorted through them, we've bagged them up, we've weighed them, we then need to look to see which ships are heading north towards the Falklands," he said.

"Then we get them on email or the radio and we say, 'Hello, would you mind taking some postcards with you?' And they're always very keen to oblige."

Author's camping trip inspired Hollywood film Wicker

'They knew she was ill - days later she killed her three kids'

Unsurprisingly, running a post office for six people does not take up all of Clarke's time at Port Lockroy.

He is also the deputy base commander, helps with the cleaning and maintenance of the site, and helps with wildlife observations for the British Antarctic Survey (BAS).

"The primary objective of the charity is conservation of the heritage surrounding UK exploration in Antarctica," Clarke said.

The team of six is about to embark on the second term of a three-year plan to shore-up and restore the island's largest building, Bransfield House, which is home to a museum, the post office and a shop.

They will install beams in the roof and 30 steel and timber props in the floor to help it withstand rain and snow.

The site on Goudier Island was chosen in the 1940s to become a permanent British foothold in Antarctica because it was known as a safe place to anchor by early 20th Century whaling ships.

The remnants of that industry are still clear to see, with the bones of whales killed long ago for their oil littering part of the shore.

Port Lockroy operated until 1962, when British research was moved to larger and more modern sites in Antarctica.

The journey from the UKAHT base in Cambridgeshire to Port Lockroy takes about a week.

"We fly to Ushuaia via Buenos Aires in Argentina and we'll probably have a couple of days to acclimatise slightly," Clarke said.

"We'll then jump on a ship that will take us south to the Antarctic Peninsula and it takes four or five days."

Clarke's colleagues are also excited to get the new season under way.

Base commander and RAF veteran Carole McCullough said: "I applied for the role looking for a bit of an adventure, and Antarctica is the ultimate adventure.

"The team work, the bonding, the appreciation of the place - it's all going to make for the most wonderful experience."

Wildlife monitor and museum manager Alice Parr added: "I actually applied for a role three years ago and was selected as reserve.

"I tried again - clearly persistence pays off! I'm incredibly excited to be managing the museum and counting penguins. It's the opportunity of a lifetime."

articles.title: Weather warnings in place but when will the storm end
articles.summary: Following the first two named storms of the season, wet and very windy conditions are set to continue into the start of the new week.
articles.body:
Storm Boelo will continue to batter parts of the UK on Sunday but the fierce autumn weather shows no sign of clearing quickly.

After two named storms in as many days, more wet and potentially very windy weather is forecast to sweep across much of the country on Monday and Tuesday.

A severe amber wind warning for Storm Boelo remains in force until Sunday evening for much of Scotland and parts of northern England. A second one in Northern Ireland expired on Sunday morning.

As the storm clears yet another area of low pressure is expected to move in from the Atlantic, although it remains uncertain whether that system will be strong enough to be named.

However, conditions could become drier and more settled later in the week as high pressure builds.

Trains cancelled and road warnings as Scotland prepares for Storm Boelo

Storm Austen brings power cuts and travel disruption as more wind and rain forecast

The UK has been hit by its first two named storms of the season, and they came within a day of each other. Storm Austen brought winds of more than 75mph on Friday, felling trees, disrupting travel and leaving some homes without power.

Storm Boelo is bringing further strong winds and heavy rain this weekend, with amber warnings in force from Saturday evening into Sunday across much of Scotland, parts of Northern Ireland and the far north of England.

Gusts could reach 80mph in exposed areas, with further travel disruption, power cuts and localised flooding possible.

There are also widespread yellow warnings for wind and rain in force across many areas of the UK on Sunday. The latest warnings are available on the BBC Weather website .

Are there signs of better weather to come?

The unsettled weather is set to continue into the start of the week, although conditions should be less severe than those seen across the country since Friday.

Another area of low pressure is expected to deepen as it approaches the UK from the south-west, bringing a further spell of heavy rain and potentially strong winds to much of the country on Monday and into Tuesday.

Rain is expected to develop from the west, with some areas potentially seeing heavy and persistent downpours. Combined with strong winds, this could lead to further travel disruption and difficult conditions, particularly in exposed coastal areas.

As with Storm Boelo, northern parts of the UK are likely to see the strongest winds and greatest impacts as Tuesday approaches. A yellow warning for wind is in place across Scotland, parts of Northern Ireland and northern England from 03:00 on Tuesday until midnight.

However, uncertainty remains over the strength and exact track of the developing low-pressure system, meaning the areas likely to experience the most severe conditions could change as the forecast evolves.

It is also not yet clear whether the system will be strong enough to be named as another storm.

You can follow the latest updates on BBC Weather online and Instagram, as well as TV and radio.

Later in the week, the weather looks set to improve for many as high pressure builds over the near continent.

That would bring more settled conditions to much of the UK, with drier and calmer weather offering a respite from the recent run of storms and unsettled weather.

articles.title: US midterms 2026: Obama urges voters to 'flip that circuit breaker', attacks Trump over 'grifting' and Iran war
articles.summary: Former President Barack Obama criticizes Donald Trump's Iran war strategy and corruption during midterm campaign rallies in Ohio and Michigan, urging voters to support Democrats for greater accountability in government.
articles.body: Former US President Barack Obama criticised Donald Trump’s handling of the Iran conflict, accused his administration of corruption and mocked its White House renovations during campaign rallies in Ohio and Michigan on Saturday, as Democrats seek to gain ground in the November 3 midterm elections.Obama urged voters to support Democratic candidates, describing the elections as an opportunity to limit the Trump administration’s actions and demand greater accountability from the government.Speaking at a rally in Michigan for US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, Obama called the November 3 vote a “circuit breaker” that could “at least rein in some of the foolishness” of Trump’s presidency.“We got to flip that circuit breaker, bring some accountability to this government,” he said.The former president also accused Trump of using his office for personal gain and criticised Republicans for backing the administration.“We have never seen a president excel in straight-up grifting, on your dime, like this,” Obama said. “Never seen a president so intent on selling favors like this ... Now the party seems to stand for corrupt government, or inept government, or no government.”Obama, who served as president from 2009 until Trump took office in 2017, remains a prominent figure among Democrats. His campaign appearances are intended to mobilise Democratic voters ahead of elections that will determine control of Congress.In Michigan, he campaigned for El-Sayed, who is facing Republican Mike Rogers, a former US representative, in a closely contested Senate race. Obama also addressed supporters in Cleveland, Ohio, where he continued his criticism of the Republican administration.The rallies came after Trump urged voters to treat the midterm elections as a referendum on his presidency, despite his name not appearing on the ballot. With control of Congress at stake, both parties are seeking to energise their supporters in the final days of campaigning.Obama challenges Trump’s Iran strategyObama questioned the administration’s claims of success in its conflict with Iran, arguing that the war had strengthened Tehran’s economic leverage by increasing uncertainty around shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global oil supplies.“Iran now has veto power over the Strait of Hormuz, where oil goes through to get to the world,” Obama said.His remarks focused on the strategic consequences of Iran’s threats against shipping in the strait, which have unsettled oil exporters. articles.title: In 1875, silver and gold created Animas Forks in Colorado's mountains; after economic downturns and two fires, only nine historic buildings remained

articles.body: Animas Forks, a former mining settlement high in Colorado’s San Juan Mountains, grew rapidly after prospectors discovered valuable mineral deposits in the surrounding area. Established in the 1870s, the remote town attracted miners, businesses and families hoping to benefit from the silver and gold boom. But its growth came with considerable challenges, including extreme winter weather, declining mining profits and destructive fires. Over time, these pressures emptied the settlement, leaving only 9 historic buildings as reminders of a community that once supported hundreds of people.Silver and gold turn Animas Forks into a mining townAccording to History Colorado, Animas Forks was established in 1875 and developed into a centre for hard-rock silver and gold prospecting. However, the settlement's beginnings date back to 1873, when prospectors built the first cabin in the area, as documented by Western Mining History.The settlement took its name from its location near the forks of the Animas River. Originally known as Three Forks of the Animas, the community adopted the shorter name Animas Forks in 1875 to accommodate the US Post Office Department, according to HistoryNet.The surrounding mountains contained mineral deposits that attracted people seeking work and investment opportunities. A wagon road built by transportation entrepreneur Otto Mears in 1875 improved connections between Animas Forks and other mining communities, helping people and supplies reach the remote settlement.By 1876, the camp had developed into an active mining community with around 30 cabins, a hotel, a general store, a saloon and a post office, according to Western Mining History. These facilities served the miners working in the surrounding districts and helped transform a small prospecting camp into a more established settlement.A growing community faced tough life at high altitudeAnimas Forks stood at an elevation of approximately 11,200 feet, making it one of the highest mining settlements in the American West. Its location offered access to mineral-rich areas, but the same mountainous surroundings made everyday life difficult.Western Mining History records that a severe blizzard in 1884 lasted 23 days and left around 25 feet of snow across the settlement. Residents had to dig tunnels through the snow to travel between buildings. The extreme conditions disrupted normal activities and demonstrated how exposed the town was to mountain weather.The cold also shaped the community's seasonal routine. Many residents moved to the lower, warmer town of Silverton each autumn, returning when conditions improved.Despite these difficulties, Animas Forks continued to attract residents. By 1883, its population had reached approximately 450, according to Western Mining History. The town supported shops, drinking establishments and other businesses that served both permanent residents and the seasonal mining workforce. Its newspaper, the Animas Forks Pioneer, began publication in 1882 and continued until October 1886.Fires and falling mining profits weakened the settlementThe town's early success depended heavily on mining, leaving it vulnerable when the industry struggled. According to the National Trust for Historic Preservation, the settlement's population began declining in the 1910s after reaching about 400 people during its more prosperous years.Mining activity had already weakened by the late 1880s. The arrival of the Silverton Northern Railroad in 1896 brought renewed interest by connecting Animas Forks with Silverton, but the railway did not expand as originally anticipated.Fires also inflicted serious damage. Mountain Studies Institute's historical account records that a devastating fire in 1891 destroyed 14 of the town's approximately 30 buildings, leaving the settlement virtually abandoned. The destruction damaged its commercial centre and dealt a major blow to local businesses.A later revival briefly offered hope. Construction of the Gold Prince Mill began in 1905, bringing workers and renewed economic activity to the area. The large industrial facility was intended to process ore from nearby mines, helping support another period of mining-related employment.However, the improvement did not last. The mill closed in 1910, and most of its machinery was removed in 1917 for use at a new facility in nearby Eureka, according to Western Mining History. A second major fire in 1913 further damaged the town, accelerating its decline.Nine historic buildings preserve the town's mining pastBy the 1920s, Animas Forks had become a ghost town. The departure of mining workers and businesses left buildings exposed to years of harsh weather, neglect and damage.According to History Colorado, 9 buildings remain at the historic townsite. Together, they provide a glimpse of the settlement's former life and the architecture used in remote mining communities during the late 19th and early 20th centuries.Among the best-known structures is the Duncan House, built in 1879. The historic jail is an important surviving building. Constructed with thick wooden walls, the jail had 2 cells and served the community when the town was active.Other surviving structures include former homes and a miner's boarding house. The remains of the Gold Prince Mill also mark the location of the industrial operation that briefly revived the settlement's fortunes in the early 20th century.Preservation efforts are giving Animas Forks a futureAlthough mining no longer supports a resident community, Animas Forks has gained renewed importance as a historic destination. Its surviving buildings form part of the Alpine Loop, a 65-mile route connecting mountain communities and historic sites in southwestern Colorado.The National Trust for Historic Preservation has documented how the settlement's popularity created new challenges. Increased visitor numbers, harsh weather and vandalism placed pressure on structures that had already endured more than a century of exposure.Preservation work has therefore become essential to the site's survival. History Colorado records that 4 of the 9 remaining buildings required stabilisation when the site received preservation funding. Such work helps protect the structures from further deterioration and keeps the settlement's history accessible to visitors.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Iran’s authorities take ‘self-sacrifice’ mobilisation campaign nationwide
articles.summary: The IRGC says it wants to use main squares in every capital of Iran’s 31 provinces for the Janfada campaign.
articles.body:
Iran’s authorities are increasing investment in a campaign to arm and train civilians who would serve in the state security apparatus against domestic and foreign threats amid growing fears that fighting with the United States and Israel could resume imminently.

The public mobilisation drive – called Janfada, or “those who sacrifice their life” – was launched in late March at the peak of the war with the US and Israel. It has now spread to large parts of the country and is aiming to attract volunteer men and women. It has a stated focus on youth but is open to all ages.

At their numerous street booths and stations, representatives of the Basij militia of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and other state bodies offer training on using weapons and other equipment to defend the government and its “revolutionary” values.

State-organised events and armed “exercises” linked with the mobilisation campaign have been held in Tehran, Isfahan, Zanjan, Shiraz, Kerman, Mashhad, Bojnord, Ahvaz and other big and small cities across many of Iran’s 31 provinces.

Ali Kowsari, Basij’s deputy for training, announced during a news conference this month that the IRGC wants to use at least 14 main squares across Tehran as training and equipment stations for Janfada volunteers. The goal is to use at least one to three squares in the capital city of every single province, he said, without divulging how many cities are currently being used as part of the campaign.

State-run nighttime events are sometimes held with rallies and motorcades during the day. A resident of Gilan province in northern Iran told Al Jazeera that people regularly see state-run stations on the streets in big and smaller cities across the province during their commutes.

“Sometimes they hold competitions to win some small prizes. They bring in live bullets, teach people how to load them into magazines, how to arm pistols and assault rifles, and how to aim and fire,” the resident said, asking to remain anonymous for security reasons.

“The organisers are mostly old men. Since the start of the war, they’ve gathered around the main square almost every night, also often playing revolutionary tunes and chanting from loudspeakers.”

In Gilan’s city of Rasht on October 15, residents objected to the noise and blocking of the street for the nighttime pro-government gathering. Videos circulating on social media showed a confrontation that escalated into a brawl although the authorities did not comment.

On Saturday, authorities cautioned residents in Alborz province’s Karaj near Tehran that they could expect explosions and loud noises from one of the Janfada exercises.

Last week, there was a big mobilisation campaign in northwestern Iran’s Kurdistan province, which borders Iraq.

The IRGC-linked Tasnim News Agency characterised a procession in the provincial capital, Sanandaj, as an exercise in “unity” between the Shia and Sunni Muslim populations.

But a number of foreign-based Iranian human rights groups have characterised such armed mobilisation efforts as “intimidation” campaigns that are held months after January’s nationwide protests, during which thousands of civilians, including many young people, were killed from gunshots and stab wounds.

The government has acknowledged that protests took place in more than 400 counties across all provinces but describes them as a “coup” attempt wholly orchestrated by the US and Israel to overthrow the establishment. It also rejected findings by an independent United Nations fact-finding mission that said the authorities committed crimes against humanity while cracking down on the protests.

Mehran Kamrava, a professor of government at Georgetown University in Qatar, said the US-Israeli war on Iran has “presented another opening for the more revolutionary elements of the Iranian body politic”.

“Revolutions are like riding a bicycle. To avoid a nasty fall, you must pedal hard. And this is precisely what the Janfadas and their leaders are trying to do – to remain relevant,” he told Al Jazeera.

“The Janfada’s training mobilisation also gives the more revolutionary-minded figures within the Iranian leadership a chance for choreographed displays of political and ideological loyalty to the revolution and its principles,” the professor said.

The government said 33 million Iranians have signed up on the campaign’s website but has provided no evidence to support this number.

It represents more than a third of the country’s population, or more than half of the over-12 population, men and women.

Earlier this year, foreign-based activists accessed the website’s source code, which showed that fewer than four million people had registered. Only a phone number was required for registration, and no national identification number was needed.

Speaking last week about the political goals of the campaign, Nematollah Bagheri, IRGC commander for the province of Lorestan, said: “The aim is to show that, just as the government supports the people, the people support the Islamic Republic and the Islamic revolution.”

Organisers said registrants could be used in future rescue operations and for social services and media and financial support. The government has also asked them to help ease the pressure of the US war, naval blockade and sanctions by consuming less fuel, electricity and other resources.

The establishment’s efforts to expand the campaign have only grown after nearly eight months of attritional war, which has killed thousands of people, made Iranians poorer and seen parts of the country’s civilian infrastructure destroyed.

Children have become a major focus for the campaign, and schools have increasingly been accommodating mobilisation. Last week, Education Minister Alireza Kazemi said the Basij militia was registering “student Janfadas” and had plans for more mobilisation and ceremonies involving children over the coming weeks.

Kamrava, the university professor, said this kind of mobilisation does not necessarily broaden the scope of the state’s legitimacy among the larger society.

“It does, however, serve to deepen the legitimacy that the state already has among its existing supporters. It reinforces belief in the revolution’s ideological and political mission and reifies the siege mentality that all revolutionaries have,” he said.

articles.title: ‘Nuclear threat will overshadow all’: Netanyahu’s Iran warning ahead of polls
articles.summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has shared a warning by author Yuval Blumberg that Israel must use the remaining two years of US President
articles.body: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has shared a warning by author Yuval Blumberg that Israel must use the remaining two years of US President Donald Trump’s term to address what Blumberg describes as an existential threat from Iran, arguing that domestic political disputes should not distract the country from the Iranian nuclear threat.Netanyahu posted an image depicting an atomic bomb over Tel Aviv on his X account alongside Blumberg’s statement. The post comes two days before Israel’s October 27 parliamentary election, as Netanyahu seeks to make national security and his relationship with Trump central to his re-election campaign.Blumberg argued that the remaining period of Trump’s presidency represents a critical opportunity for Israel to pursue its objectives against Iran. He questioned what might happen after Trump leaves office in 2028 and whether a successor would provide the same level of support.In the statement shared by Netanyahu, Blumberg said future generations would not forgive Israel’s current leadership if it missed what he described as a historic opportunity to address the Iranian threat. He also argued that Israel’s resources should be directed towards that mission.Blumberg also invoked the possibility of a nuclear attack on Israel, arguing that Iran’s acquisition of atomic weapons would overshadow all other political disputes. He described controversies involving Qatar, the ultra-Orthodox Jewish community and military conscription as distractions from what he considers Israel’s most pressing security challenge.He also criticised Netanyahu’s potential successors, arguing that a prime minister unable to maintain close ties with Trump or withstand domestic political pressure would struggle to complete the mission against Iran. Blumberg urged voters to prioritise national security over political opposition to Netanyahu, warning of catastrophic consequences if Israel missed the current opportunity.The remarks come amid heightened political debate over Israel’s security policy ahead of the October 27 election. Trump endorsed Netanyahu’s re-election bid on October 18, reinforcing the Israeli prime minister’s argument that their partnership is important to confronting Iran.You use AI every day.
